deptLabel: NYC Department of Health & Mental Hygiene
pageDescription: How to navigate Community Health Profiles, understand the data, and get the most from the site.
intro: Community Health Profiles is a public data tool from the NYC Department of Health. It presents health indicators for all 59 of the city's community districts, with comparisons to borough and citywide values, so communities, researchers, and policymakers can see how their neighborhood compares and where disparities exist.

navigating.choosingNeighborhood: Every profile is scoped to a single community district. Use the search box at the top of the left sidebar to find one by neighborhood name, borough, community district number, or street address — typing 'Bronx' lists every Bronx district, and typing an address like '123 Main St Brooklyn' finds the district that contains it. Clicking into the empty search box shows the full list, grouped by borough. On a larger screen you can also click any district on the sidebar map. On a phone, tap the neighborhood name at the top of the page to open the same search.
navigating.topicNavigation: The bar near the top of the page lists the main health topics. Hovering a topic opens a list of its subtopics; clicking a topic or subtopic scrolls straight to it. As you scroll, the current topic is highlighted and the thin bar underneath shows where you are (Topic › Subtopic).
navigating.findingIndicator: Switch to the Indicator tab in the left sidebar to search every indicator by name. Results are grouped by subtopic, and choosing one scrolls the page directly to that indicator's chart.

comparing.p1: Every profile shows one neighborhood at a time, but you can add a second community district to compare against. On a larger screen, use the 'Compare to' field in the sidebar's Neighborhood tab. On a phone, tap the Compare button at the top of the page. Search for any other district and select it.
comparing.p2: Once a comparison district is selected, it is highlighted in orange on every bar chart on the page, while your primary neighborhood stays highlighted in purple. Both values are labeled directly on each chart. The sidebar map also shows both districts in the same colors, so you can see where they sit relative to each other.
comparing.p3: The comparison district's name appears as a pill under 'Compare to'. Click the name to choose a different district, or click the × to clear it and return to the single-neighborhood view.

nonObvious.intro: A few useful interactions aren't labeled on the page — they're worth knowing about.

understandingData.communityDistricts: New York City is divided into 59 community districts — administrative units that roughly correspond to neighborhoods. Each district has its own community board and typically covers 50,000–200,000 residents. Profiles use these districts because they reflect meaningful local boundaries and because much of the city's health data is collected and reported at this level.
understandingData.indicators: Each measure shown is called an indicator — a single, well-defined measure of a health-related condition in a population. Examples include the share of adults with diagnosed diabetes, the rate of avoidable hospitalizations, or life expectancy at birth. Indicators are chosen because they can be measured reliably, compared across neighborhoods, and help explain population health.
understandingData.comparisons: Most indicators are compared with the citywide value. 'Higher' or 'lower' than citywide tells you how this district compares with the city as a whole — not whether the result is good or bad in absolute terms. For some indicators (like poverty) lower is better; for others (like life expectancy) higher is better. Where that direction is known, the comparison label is colored to show whether the difference is favorable or unfavorable.
understandingData.readingCharts: Most indicators are shown as a bar chart with one bar per community district, sorted from lowest to highest. Your neighborhood's bar is purple and a comparison district's bar is orange; all others are gray. A dashed line marks the citywide value (it's left off for indicators that are simple counts, where a citywide total isn't a useful reference). Hover or tap any bar to see that district's name and value. The expanded view adds the borough and citywide values to the legend.
understandingData.smallNumbers: Some values are based on small numbers of people or survey responses. Where an estimate may be unreliable, the details panel notes that it should be interpreted with caution. To protect privacy, some very small values are suppressed: those districts have no value label on the chart and are listed as '(Suppressed)' in the chart legend, with a note explaining why.

detailPanel.intro: Every indicator chart has a Details button in its top-right corner. Clicking it — or clicking the chart's short description — opens a side panel (or a pull-up sheet on a phone) with more context:
detailPanel.choropleth: A map of all 59 community districts shaded by their value for this indicator, from light (lowest) to dark (highest). A plain-language sentence below the map compares your neighborhood with the city.
detailPanel.barChart: Below the map is the same bar chart shown on the card. Hovering a district on the map highlights its bar in the chart, and the other way around.
detailPanel.sourceDescription: The data source and year. Click the ? next to the source for full notes, including a plain-language description of what the indicator measures and a link to the source data where available.

sharing.intro: Charts and data can be saved, shared, or reused in a few ways:
sharing.export: Open a chart's Details panel and choose Export, or, on a larger screen, click the expand icon in the chart's bottom-right corner to open a bigger view. From either one you can copy the chart image, download it as a PNG, or get code to embed the chart on another website.
sharing.data: You can download the data behind any chart as a CSV file. Choose CSV from the Export button in the chart's Details panel, or from the chart's expanded view. The file includes every community district's value for that indicator, along with the borough and citywide values. Suppressed values have an empty value column and are marked 'suppressed'.
sharing.links: The copy-link icon in the bar under the topic navigation copies a link to the section you're viewing. The Details panel has its own Copy link button that links to that indicator.
sharing.print: Use 'Print this report' at the top of any neighborhood profile to open a printer-friendly version of the full profile, which you can print or save as a PDF.
sharing.language: Use the language menu in the page header to view the site in another language. Translations are automatic and may not be exact.

dataSources.p1: Indicators draw on multiple sources, including the American Community Survey, NYC vital statistics, hospital discharge records, and surveys run by the NYC Department of Health. Data years vary by indicator and are shown with each chart's source.
